list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. C
Initial evaluation includes radiography to measure the Cobb angle (). C
Individuals with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis generally do well with observation alone. B
Right curves are most common in patients with idiopathic scoliosis. Back pain and left curves should prompt concern for other spinal disease, such as tumor. C
Bracing is often used for curves of 20 to 40 degrees and are effective at halting curve progression. B

No high-quality studies support surgery for the treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Indications for surgery are largely cosmetic rather than functional and should not use the Cobb angle as the sole criteria. B

background.definition: Scoliosis is defined by a lateral curvature of the spine deviating from a normal vertical alignment. Convex curve to the right is termed dextroscoliosis and is more common than convex curve to the left (levoscoliosis). A component of rotation may also occur with scoliosis and is referred to as rotoscoliosis.

list.listitem: Idiopathic scoliosis occurs in approximately 2% to 3% of children; severe curves of greater than 40° occur in 2% to 5% of children.
In 1995, approximately 60,300 office visits were attributed to idiopathic scoliosis.

Idiopathic scoliosis is the most common type (up to 80% of cases). It presents in the juvenile, adolescent, or adult time frame and may be a genetic disorder of high prevalence and variable penetrance.
Congenital scoliosis represents approximately 10% of cases.

Scoliosis may also accompany other conditions, including cerebral palsy, spina bifida, spinal muscular atrophy, Friedrich’s ataxia, Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and CHARGE syndrome (Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia of choanae, Retardation of growth or development, Genital/urinary abnormalities, Ear abnormalities, or deafness).

The underlying pathophysiology of idiopathic scoliosis is unknown, but genetic factors are likely involved. Candidate genes located on chromosomes 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 16, 17, 19, and X have been implicated.

Congenital conditions occur during fetal development, including failure of formation of the vertebra (hemivertebra), failure of segmentation of normal vertebral bodies, or combinations of both. These instances may be accompanied by abnormalities in the genitourinary system.
Scoliosis accompanying neuromuscular disorders may occur as a side effect of muscular weakness and the inability of musculature to support the upright spine, as seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. C
Most children are asymptomatic and present as a result of school-based screening or cosmetic concerns. C
Other diseases to consider during the history and physical examination include Marfan syndrome, muscular dystrophy, and neurofibromatosis. C
Initial evaluation includes radiography to measure the Cobb angle (). C

Initial patient contact is usually as a result of routine screening by a school nurse or when a curvature is noted by parents. Patients with idiopathic scoliosis rarely have symptoms such as pain or respiratory compromise.

Physical examination should include observing the patient from the back while bending forward at the waist. The presence of an asymmetric hump on one side or other of the back may indicate the presence of scoliosis. Forward bending is more sensitive than devices such as the scoliometer.
Other findings may include shoulder and hip height discrepancy or a difference in distance between the elbow and flank when the patient stands up straight with arms at the side.

Other potentially important physical findings include: cafe-au-lait spots potentially indicating neurofibromatosis; heart murmur (Marfan syndrome); musculoskeletal abnormalities, such as spasticity from cerebral palsy; muscular weakness from muscular dystrophy or atrophy; and leg length discrepancy from compensatory scoliosis.

Right curves are most common in patients with idiopathic scoliosis. Although there may be an association between left curves and underlying disease, the association is weak. Back pain should increase concern for other spinal disease, such as tumor.
The initial evaluation should include radiographic viewing the entire spine. The angle of curvature may be measured by using either the Cobb method or Risser-Ferguson method.

The Cobb method uses the angle (referred to as the Cobb angle) formed by the intersection of two lines: one extending from the top of the vertebral body at the top of the curve and one along the bottom of the lower vertebral body (see ).

The Risser-Ferguson method uses lines through the center of the top vertebrae and bottom vertebrae and determines the angles where these two lines intersect in the center of the vertebral body at the apex of the curve.
Additional evaluation should be guided by individual patient presentation or complaint.
Referral is recommended for children with left scoliotic curve and pain, possibly indicating an underlying more serious condition.
When scoliosis is suspected, order standing posteroanterior radiographs of the entire spine from C7 to the sacrum on one film. Calculation of the Cobb angle () can define the severity of curvature.
Refer patients with more pronounced curves or who are symptomatic to an orthopedist specializing in scoliosis.
There is no evidence that supports the use of electrical stimulation, manual therapy, or chiropractic care for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. B

Scoliosis-specific exercise is not supported by high-quality evidence as an effective intervention for preventing progression of or for delaying or avoiding invasive treatments for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. B

Bracing or surgery may be considered for severe curves that cause significant pain, affect balance, gait, or respiratory function, or are associated with severe contractures in wheelchair-bound individuals. C

Bracing may reduce the progression of high-risk curves to the threshold for surgery, based on low to very low quality evidence. Bracing used in specialized centers may be more beneficial, and bracing combined with exercise. B

A beneficial effect of surgery in children with scoliosis associated with neuromuscular conditions is uncertain. No RCTs comparing surgical and nonsurgical treatments for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis have been conducted. B

Surgery is intended to correct deformity, prevent curve progression, improve function, and improve cosmetic appearance. However, a Cochrane review found no RCTs comparing surgical and nonsurgical treatments for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.

A retrospective cohort study of 341 adults with scoliosis and back pain found that patients who chose surgery had significantly improved symptom and quality of life scores compared with patients who chose nonoperative therapy after 2 years.

In a review of patients 5 years after surgical intervention, individuals reported improved self-image and function and a trend toward greater level of activity, despite an increase in pain from postoperative year 2 to year 5. No objective parameter (such as worsening curve) explained increased pain reports.

Despite the use of fusion or arthrodesis, there are no high-quality studies comparing surgery with other modes of therapy. Many postoperative comparison studies are based only on patient satisfaction scores. Therefore, the risks and benefits of surgery must be individually assessed.

In cases of neuromuscular scoliosis—including Duchenne muscular dystrophy, spina bifida, and cerebral palsy—no high-quality studies demonstrate a clinically significant benefit of surgery. The decision for surgery should be based on an evaluation of the individual patient, the capacity for ambulation, and the risk of perioperative complications.

A Cochrane review found low to very low quality evidence that antifibrinolytic agents (eg, tranexamic acid) may reduce rates of autologous and allogeneic blood transfusion during scoliosis surgery in children. However, the optimal dose, short-term safety for rare but serious adverse events, and long-term safety are uncertain.

A Cochrane review concluded that postoperative epidural analgesia, compared to systemic analgesia, for thoraco-lumbar spine surgery in children may result in modest improvement in pain up to 72 hours postoperatively, based on moderate and low quality evidence. Resumption of gastrointestinal function may also be improved.
There is no evidence supporting the use of electrical stimulation, manual therapy, or chiropractic care in the management of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
Quantified trunk rotational strength training may stabilize curves of less than 40° for short periods (approximately 8 months), but has no effect on stabilizing curves of 50° to 60°.

A systematic review of bracing versus observation found no difference in subsequent surgical intervention in children with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: 23% of children who were managed with bracing and 22% of children managed with observation alone went on to receive surgical intervention.

However, a subsequent multicenter RCT found that significantly fewer children assigned to bracing progressed to a curvature of 50° or more than children assigned to observation (NNT = 4). The bracing was more effective in those with better adherence and more daily hours of use.

In patients with an initial curvature of less than or equal to 35°, bracing using a nighttime-only device such as the Charleston or Providence brace is as effective as the 22-hour whole body thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) or cervicothoracolumbosacral (Milwaukee) brace.
Bracing in patients with curvatures greater than 35° is less effective in preventing curve progression.
For adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis wearing braces who have reached skeletal maturity, outcomes are the same for immediate weaning versus gradual weaning (typically over 6 months) of braces.
In adult scoliosis, there is no evidence that bracing improves patient-oriented outcomes, including pain or function.

There is minimal, if any, evidence to support physical therapy or exercise therapy. A Cochrane review concluded that scoliosis-specific exercise is not supported by high-quality evidence as an effective intervention for preventing progression of or for delaying or avoiding invasive treatments for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
There is some evidence that consistent adherence to an appropriately designed exercise regimen may reduce curve progression in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
Children may need emotional support, as in any chronic medical condition.
Mild idiopathic scoliosis (curve angle <10°) generally presents in adolescence, progresses slowly, and does not require treatment. B
Adults with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis report more back pain and higher cosmetic concerns, but their long-term quality of life is comparable with that of unaffected individuals. B
In patients with idiopathic scoliosis and curves between 40° and 50°, curvature progresses after skeletal maturity at the rate of approximately 1° per year. B

Curvatures with angles of less than 10° are unlikely to progress, and these individuals usually lead productive lives with low disability. Adults with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis do report more back pain and higher cosmetic concerns, but their long-term quality of life is comparable with that of unaffected individuals.
In patients with idiopathic scoliosis and curves between 40° and 50°, curvature progresses after skeletal maturity at the rate of approximately 0.5° to 1° per year.

A study followed up patients who had not been operatively treated in adolescence for a curve of at least 30° (Risser grade >= 4). Those with a single main thoracic curve had quality of life similar to that of healthy controls. However, patients with thoracolumbar or double-major scoliosis had significantly worse low back pain compared with the main thoracic group.
A Cobb angle at maturity of 50° or more increases the likelihood of shortness of breath.
Pain is more commonly reported in patients with scoliosis versus control patients, but few scoliosis patients use narcotic pain relievers.

Individuals with a Cobb curve of more than 100° are at increased risk of death from cor pulmonale and right ventricular heart failure. The cumulative death rate for all patients with untreated idiopathic scoliosis is not increased compared with that of the general population.
Curve progression is unaffected by pregnancy.
After an initial evaluation, follow-up is recommended for children with idiopathic scoliosis at 6-month intervals until growth is complete.
Growth is defined as complete after full maturation of the posterior superior iliac crest.

A study evaluated curve progression during pregnancy in women with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis treated with surgery or bracing for more than 20 years. Compared with control patients, there was no difference in cesarean delivery rates, but vacuum extractions occurred significantly more often in the surgery group. No correlation was identified between the number of pregnancies and progression of the scoliotic curve.
